title: Mead Hangover: Why Honey Wine Hits Hard and How to Avoid It
excerpt: Why mead hangovers can be so rough: high and variable strength, sweetness that hides alcohol, big horn pours, and fusel alcohols in homemade batches. Plus how to prevent and recover.
metaDescription: Why mead hangovers hit hard: strength, sugar, congeners, and big pours. How honey wine compares to wine and beer, plus how to prevent and recover.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** mead doesn't have some special hangover-causing ingredient, but it's very easy to get a bad hangover from it. Most of the blame goes to three ordinary things. Mead is often much stronger than people expect (frequently 12 to 18% alcohol, roughly wine strength or above), it's often sweet enough to hide that strength, and it tends to get poured in large servings at festivals, feasts, and Renaissance faires. Homemade mead adds a fourth risk: a stressed fermentation can produce harsh "fusel" alcohols that many people associate with rough mornings. The honey itself isn't a hangover cure, and there's no good evidence that it makes mead gentler than wine.

**The quick rules:** Check the label strength before you start, because a "honey wine" can be anywhere from beer strength to near-port strength. Treat a 5 oz glass of 12 to 14% mead like a glass of wine, and treat a full drinking horn as two to four drinks. Go slower with sweet and sparkling meads. Alternate with water, eat a real meal, and stop earlier than you would with beer. If you brew your own, a mead that tastes "hot" or solvent-like is a sign to drink less of it, not to push through.

> **When to see a doctor.** A mead hangover is usually just a hangover: headache, thirst, tiredness, and an unsettled stomach that ease within a day. **Get medical help right away** if someone who has been drinking is confused, very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, having a seizure, vomiting while not fully awake, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and you should call 911 (or your local emergency number). See a doctor soon if you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, see blood in vomit or stool, have severe belly pain, or your symptoms aren't improving after 24 hours. If you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious every time you stop drinking, mention it to a doctor. That pattern is worth a conversation, and it's easy to help with when caught early. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Mead Hangovers Can Hit So Hard

Mead is one of the oldest alcoholic drinks there is. At its simplest it's honey, water, and yeast, fermented until the yeast has turned much of the honey's sugar into alcohol. That simple recipe hides a lot of variety, and the variety is what catches people out.

### 1. It's often stronger than it looks

Honey is almost pure sugar, so there's a lot of fuel for the yeast. A traditional still mead commonly lands somewhere around 12 to 14% alcohol, and stronger "sack" meads can run higher, sometimes into the high teens. Lighter "session" meads and hydromels sit closer to beer or cider strength, often in the 4 to 8% range. The bottle may look like cider, the drink may taste like dessert, and the strength may match a big red wine.

Here is what that means in practice. In the US, one standard drink contains about 0.6 fluid ounces of pure alcohol. Using that measure:

- **A 5 oz glass of 12% mead** is about 1 standard drink.
- **A 5 oz glass of 16% mead** is about 1.3 standard drinks.
- **A 12 oz bottle of 6% session mead** is about 1.2 standard drinks.
- **A 16 oz drinking horn of 14% mead** is about 3.7 standard drinks.
- **A 750 ml bottle of 14% mead** is roughly 6 standard drinks.

That horn is the part people miss. At festivals and themed events, mead often comes in horns, tankards, or large plastic cups, and two "drinks" can quietly be seven or eight standard drinks. The size of your hangover tracks closely with how much alcohol you took in, so this is usually the single biggest reason a mead night goes badly.

### 2. Sweetness hides the alcohol

Many meads are finished semi-sweet or sweet. Sugar softens the burn of alcohol, so a 14% sweet mead can go down as easily as juice. Sweet drinks are easy to sip quickly, and drinking faster raises your blood alcohol level faster, which is closely tied to how rough the next morning feels.

There's a related question about whether the sugar itself makes a hangover worse. The honest answer is that there's no good evidence that residual sugar in a drink, on its own, causes a worse hangover. What sugar clearly does is make it easier to drink more, faster. Some people also find very sweet drinks leave them with an upset stomach or a sugary "crash" feeling the next day, but that's a personal pattern rather than a well-studied effect.

### 3. Sparkling mead may hit you sooner

Some meads are carbonated, either naturally in the bottle or by force-carbonation. Small studies on carbonated drinks have suggested that bubbles can speed up how fast alcohol is absorbed in some people, though the effect is not consistent from person to person. It's the same idea behind the reputation of champagne for "going straight to your head." If you notice sparkling mead seems to hit harder, slow your pace. Our [champagne hangover guide](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) explains the bubble effect in more detail.

### 4. Congeners and fusel alcohols, especially in homemade mead

Congeners are the by-products of fermentation other than the main alcohol (ethanol). They include small amounts of methanol, other "higher" alcohols (often called fusel alcohols), aldehydes, and esters. They're part of what gives each drink its flavor, and research on hangovers has generally found that drinks higher in congeners, such as bourbon, tend to produce worse hangovers than very clean spirits such as vodka at the same alcohol dose. Our [guide to congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) covers that research.

There isn't much published research measuring congeners in mead specifically, so nobody can honestly tell you whether mead is a "high" or "low" congener drink as a category. What mead makers do know is that honey is low in the nutrients yeast needs. When yeast is short on nutrients or ferments too warm, it gets stressed and tends to produce more fusel alcohols. That's why poorly made mead can taste "hot," harsh, or a bit like solvent, and why it often needs months of aging to smooth out.

Commercial meaderies manage this with yeast nutrients, temperature control, and aging. Homebrewed mead varies a lot. If your homemade batch tastes hot or burning beyond its strength, that's a reasonable sign it's high in fusels, and many people find those batches give them worse mornings. It's not a reason to throw it out, but it is a reason to drink it slowly and in smaller amounts, or to let it age longer.

A note on methanol: honey has very little pectin, which is the fruit fiber that breaks down into methanol during fermentation. So plain mead isn't thought to be a high-methanol drink. Meads made with lots of fruit (called melomels) carry a bit more, similar to fruit wines. In normal fermented drinks, methanol is present only in small amounts and is not a safety concern at typical drinking levels. The real methanol danger comes from badly made distilled spirits, not from fermented mead.

### 5. Sulfites and other additives

Honey doesn't naturally contain added sulfites, but many commercial meads, like most wines, have sulfites added to protect them from spoilage. Sweet meads are also often stabilized with potassium sorbate so they don't re-ferment in the bottle. These are common, well-studied additives. For most people, sulfites are not a meaningful cause of hangovers or headaches. A small number of people are genuinely sensitive to sulfites, and for them the typical reaction is breathing trouble, flushing, or hives rather than a classic hangover. Our article on [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) goes through what the evidence does and doesn't support. If you're sulfite-sensitive, look for meads labeled without added sulfites, and check with your doctor if you've ever had breathing symptoms from wine.

## Honey Wine, Sugar, and Congeners: What Actually Matters

Because "honey wine" sounds natural and gentle, a lot of people assume mead must be kinder to the body than other drinks. Here's how each piece really stacks up.

**Honey doesn't cancel out the alcohol.** Once fermented, most or all of the honey's sugar has become alcohol, at least in a dry mead. Whatever is left behind is sweetness, not protection. Your liver processes the alcohol in mead exactly the way it processes the alcohol in wine, beer, or spirits: first into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that contributes to hangover symptoms, and then into acetate.

**The sugar-and-alcohol "fructose trick" isn't a reliable fix.** You may have seen claims that the fructose in honey helps your body clear alcohol faster. Some older lab and small human studies explored whether fructose speeds alcohol metabolism, with mixed results. There is no good evidence that the sugar left in mead, or eating honey, will meaningfully lower your blood alcohol or prevent a hangover.

**Congeners vary more by how the mead is made than by the honey.** A clean, well-aged commercial mead and a rushed, warm-fermented homebrew can be very different drinks even with the same honey and the same strength. Dark, flavor-heavy honeys like buckwheat produce richer meads, but there's no good evidence that honey variety by itself changes how bad your hangover will be.

**Dry vs sweet.** A dry mead has had more of its sugar fermented away, which usually means it's at the higher end of the strength range for its recipe. A sweet mead may be a little lower in alcohol or the same strength with sugar added back. Neither style is hangover-proof. The safest assumption is that any mead is about as strong as wine until the label tells you otherwise.

## Mead vs Wine vs Beer: Is Mead Worse?

For the same amount of alcohol, there's no good evidence that mead gives you a worse hangover than wine. The difference people notice usually comes from how mead is drunk, not what it is.

- **Compared with beer:** a pint of 14% mead holds roughly three times the alcohol of a pint of 5% beer. If you drink mead at a beer pace, you'll feel it. See our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) for how beer compares.
- **Compared with wine:** strength is similar to a little higher, and serving habits are the main risk. A wine glass of mead is a reasonable comparison. A horn of mead is not.
- **Compared with cider:** some meads look and are sold like cider, especially sparkling hydromels. Others are three times cider strength. Always check the label.

The [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) covers a lot of what applies to mead too, since both are fermented, often sweetened, sometimes sparkling, and usually poured in similar glasses at home.

## Why Mead Nights Often End in Bad Mornings

The setting matters as much as the drink. Mead tends to show up at:

- **Renaissance faires, medieval festivals, and outdoor events**, often in warm weather, in the sun, with lots of walking and not much water.
- **Feasts and themed parties**, where horns get refilled and nobody counts.
- **Meadery tasting rooms and flights**, where several small pours of strong mead add up quickly.
- **Homebrew sharing**, where the strength of each bottle is often a guess.

Heat and sun increase fluid loss through sweat. Long days on your feet and irregular meals mean you're often drinking on an emptier stomach than you think. Alcohol also suppresses a hormone that helps your kidneys hold on to water, so you pee more than you drink. None of these is unique to mead, but they cluster around it.

## How to Enjoy Mead Without Wrecking Tomorrow

None of these steps are exotic. They work because they lower how much alcohol you take in and how fast.

1. **Read the strength.** Look for the ABV (alcohol by volume) on the label or ask at the bar. If it's homebrewed, assume wine strength or higher.
2. **Use a wine glass, not a horn.** A 4 to 5 oz pour lets you count drinks honestly. If you have a horn, fill it partway.
3. **Pace yourself.** A useful rough guide is no more than about one standard drink per hour, which is roughly how fast an average adult's liver clears alcohol (it varies a lot from person to person).
4. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between each glass of mead slows you down and helps with thirst. In hot weather, drink more water than you think you need.
5. **Eat first and keep eating.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream. A proper meal beats festival snacks.
6. **Be extra careful with sweet and sparkling meads.** These are the easiest to drink too quickly.
7. **Don't mix in heavy spirits.** Mead plus shots is how a manageable evening becomes a lost morning. The common rule about drink order is a myth (our [beer before liquor explainer](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) covers why), but total alcohol isn't.
8. **Stop earlier with harsh-tasting homebrew.** If it burns more than its strength explains, sip it, don't drink it.

For a broader plan, our [guide on how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through the full approach.

## Already Hungover From Mead? What Helps

There's no instant fix, but you can feel better faster.

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water through the morning. If you were sweating at an outdoor event or you've been vomiting, an oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix can help more than plain water. Our piece on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) explains when they're worth it.
- **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, rice, or broth are easy on an unsettled stomach and help steady low energy.
- **Treat the headache carefully.** If you use a pain reliever, follow the label. Ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already upset, so take them with food. Avoid taking acetaminophen (Tylenol) while alcohol is still in your system or if you drink heavily on a regular basis. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why. If you're unsure which is right for you, ask a pharmacist.
- **Rest.** Alcohol disrupts the second half of the night's sleep, so you're likely short on real rest even if you were in bed a long time. A nap helps.
- **Skip "hair of the dog."** Another drink only delays the hangover and adds more alcohol for your liver to deal with.
- **Give it time.** Most hangovers fade within 24 hours. If yours is getting worse rather than better, or you have any of the warning signs in the box at the top, get medical advice.

## Is Honey Itself Good for a Hangover?

Eating honey the morning after isn't harmful for most people, and a bit of easy sugar can help if you feel weak or shaky from not eating. Beyond that, there's no good evidence that honey speeds hangover recovery. It's fine as part of breakfast, not as a treatment. The same goes for any idea that drinking more mead "because it's just honey" will help. It won't.

## A Note on Homemade Mead Safety

Mead is one of the most popular homebrew projects, and well-made homemade mead is generally safe. A few practical points:

- **Fermentation doesn't produce dangerous methanol levels** in normal mead. The real methanol risk is in home distillation, which is a different and riskier activity (and illegal without a license in many places, including the US).
- **Strength is hard to judge by taste.** Use a hydrometer if you want to know how strong your batch is, and label bottles so friends know what they're drinking.
- **Bottle bombs are a bigger risk than poisoning.** Sweet mead bottled before fermentation has finished can keep producing gas and burst. Stabilize or make sure fermentation is complete before bottling.
- **Spoiled mead usually smells or tastes clearly wrong** (vinegar, rotten, moldy). Don't drink a batch that has visible mold.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who enjoy mead, wine, or beer look at supplements to support their body on nights they drink. The one we cover most on this site is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis) that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver.

It's worth being clear about what that research shows. Most of it comes from animal and lab studies, which have reported effects on alcohol-related changes in the brain and liver. Human research is still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone, and it doesn't change how much alcohol is in a glass of mead or make heavy drinking safe. It's an optional add-on to the basics above, not a replacement for them.

If you want to try it, a straightforward, well-reviewed option is [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing. Check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you take regular medications, are pregnant, or have a health condition.

## The Bottom Line

Mead isn't uniquely evil, and honey doesn't make it gentle. A mead hangover is mostly about how much alcohol you drank, how fast you drank it, and whether you were eating and drinking water. Mead's high and variable strength, its easy-drinking sweetness, the big servings that come with festivals and feasts, and the harsh fusel alcohols in some homebrew all push those numbers the wrong way. Check the strength, pour wine-sized servings, slow down with sweet and sparkling styles, and keep water and food nearby. If anything about the morning after feels more serious than a hangover, get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does mead give you a worse hangover than wine?**

For the same amount of alcohol, there's no good evidence that it does. Mead often feels worse because it's frequently stronger than people expect, it's easy to drink quickly when sweet, and it's often served in large horns or cups. Count your drinks by strength and pour size, not by the number of refills.

**Why does mead give me such a bad headache?**

The most likely reasons are simply more alcohol than you realized and dehydration, especially at outdoor events. Harsh homemade mead may also be higher in fusel alcohols, which many people associate with worse hangovers. Sulfites are an unlikely cause for most people. Drink water alongside mead, use smaller pours, and if headaches happen even after small amounts, mention it to a doctor.

**How strong is mead?**

It varies a lot. Light session meads and hydromels can be around 4 to 8% alcohol, similar to beer or cider. Traditional meads often sit around 12 to 14%, and stronger sack meads can reach the high teens. Always check the label, and assume homemade mead is at least wine strength.

**Does the sugar in mead make hangovers worse?**

There's no good evidence that the leftover sugar itself causes a worse hangover. The bigger issue is that sweetness hides the taste of alcohol, so it's easy to drink more and faster. Some people do feel worse after very sweet drinks, so if you notice that pattern, choose a drier mead or drink less of the sweet ones.

**Is homemade mead more likely to cause a hangover?**

It can be. Honey is low in the nutrients yeast needs, and a stressed or warm fermentation tends to produce more fusel alcohols, which give mead a hot, harsh taste. Many people find those batches harder on them the next day. Homemade mead is also often stronger than anyone realizes. Aging the mead and drinking it slowly helps.

**Can mead make you sick in a dangerous way?**

Normal fermented mead doesn't contain dangerous levels of methanol. The main danger is the same as with any alcohol: drinking too much too fast. Call 911 if someone is confused, can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or is vomiting while barely conscious. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning.

**How many drinks is a horn of mead?**

It depends on the horn and the mead, but a 16 oz horn of 14% mead holds about 3.7 US standard drinks. Even a smaller 10 to 12 oz horn of wine-strength mead is two or more drinks. If you're drinking from a horn, fill it partway and drink water between refills.

**Does DHM help with a mead hangover?**

DHM has interesting research on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. There's no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone, and it doesn't make drinking a lot of strong mead safe. If you try it, use it alongside pacing, food, and water, and check with a doctor if you take other medications.
